caption:
Was the Cardiff Giant real? No — and the man who made it said so himself.

On October 16, 1869, two men hired to dig a well behind William Newell's barn in Cardiff, New York, found a ten-foot stone man. Newell put a tent over it and charged fifty cents for fifteen minutes. Three to five hundred people a day came.

The giant was made by George Hull, a New York tobacconist. He had lost an argument at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4 and the giants it says once lived on Earth. He wanted to prove how easily people could be fooled.

In 1868 Hull had a gypsum block quarried at Fort Dodge, Iowa, telling the workmen it was for a Lincoln monument. Sculptors in Chicago carved it in Hull's own likeness, hanging quilts to muffle the sound. He learned from a geologist that hair does not petrify, so the figure has none. Sand, sulphuric acid and steel knitting needles aged the surface and faked the pores.

Andrew D. White of Cornell noticed the simplest flaw: there was no reason to dig a well on that spot, with a good spring already running to house and barn. Yale's O. C. Marsh called it "a most decided humbug" — soluble gypsum with fresh tool marks. Hull confessed on December 10, 1869.

What remains unresolved: whether the Chicago stonecutter who took the commission ever knew what it was for. And the famous line about a sucker born every minute was said by David Hannum, who owned the giant, not by Barnum, who copied it.

Images: the giant photographed by Bain News Service, 1910; "The Onondaga Giant," Popular Graphic Arts; and both sides of an 1873 stereocard of the Fort Dodge gypsum quarry, from the New York Public Library.
